title_original: Living Memory at the Bourse de Commerce
excerpt_original: At the Bourse de Commerce in Paris, the Pinault Collection puts photography center stage with “Remember Me,” a choral exhibition where iconic artists meet visual experiments. L’article Living Memory at the Bourse de Commerce est apparu en premier sur Blind Magazine .

blocks.text: “Divided into four chapters, the ‘Remember Me’ exhibition makes it possible to show the prints of the Pinault Collection on a scale unprecedented in Paris,” says curator Matthieu Humery by way of introduction. As events marking the bicentenary of photography multiply, the Bourse de Commerce is showing, until January 18, 2027, more than 700 images from the 8,000 held by the collector. It is an opportunity to approach the visit with a double perspective: “understanding what is at stake in the image today, but also understanding the Pinault holdings,” he adds. Tracing the history of photography from its invention to the present day, the exhibition alternates group hangs and solo shows, sitting perfectly within the grandeur of the building, to question the capacity of photographs to “challenge us in a world where they proliferate, while paying tribute to an art and its ability to speak to us.”

At the very center of the museum, The History of Tears , a work by Barbara Kruger conceived specifically for the architecture of the rotunda, opens the show. Monumental, the installation sets words (those of George Orwell, Roland Barthes and Aimé Césaire) against powerful emotions. Pasted across the walls, the sentences collide with videos in a strange kind of dialogue where domination, anger and joy blend depending on the reading one chooses. “The three literary quotations make it possible to understand the logic behind the conception of the space. There is the political dimension, the romantic dimension, and the desire to resolve conflict,” explains Matthieu Humery.

Gallery 2 then plunges us into the world of Irving Penn. Here, 450 photographs dating from the 1940s to the 2000s line the upper reaches of the white walls, winding to the very limits of our vision. The effect is dizzying. “The idea here is to show the artist’s work in its entirety rather than by theme or series. To do this, I played with the notion of immensity: I wanted visitors entering the room to be unable to see its end,” the curator confides. Gelatin silver and palladium prints, in color and in black and white, are arranged along the walls, forming mysterious connections: so many nods to a secret narrative thread that one gets lost trying to uncover.

One floor up, Raymond Depardon’s “La France” takes the opposite approach to this avalanche of images. Here, the photographs, made with a large-format view camera, follow a route conceived as a reference to the photographer’s own approach. “He wanted to turn his gaze on a France in transformation that we never look at. From 2004 to 2010, he traveled the country in a van and chose to take only one shot per location,” says Matthieu Humery. The result is a body of 300 images, 50 of which are shown in “Remember Me”: the fruit of long-term work in which the immediacy of composition meets the slowness imposed by the chosen technique. Hung on the walls, but also on either side of the room and suspended from the ceiling, the photographs seem, through their arrangement, to invite us on a kind of journey to discover them better.

On the top floor of the Bourse de Commerce, the group show brings the exhibition to a close. It is organized into several themes: “By the Sea,” “Sérialité et typologie” (Seriality and Typology), “La fabrique de l’image” (The Making of the Image), “L’art de la composition” (The Art of Composition), “Le langage des mains” (The Language of Hands), “Face à face” (Face to Face) and “Le corps révélé” (The Body Revealed). Together they offer a selection of emblematic prints rooted in a rich photographic history. From one gallery to the next, big names rub shoulders with visual experiments; artists draw inspiration from one another, exchange nods and explore new ways of creating. Among them is an 1854 image by Roger Fenton, the oldest in the collection, which owes much to the paintings of Turner.

Further on, visitors come across Man Ray’s solarizations and Weegee’s distortions, Annie Leibovitz’s iconic portrait of John Lennon and Yoko Ono, and portraits by August Sander printed by his son. There is also a sculpture by Brancusi that inspired Man Ray’s famous Noire et Blanche (1926), a motif taken up by Edward Steichen with his model Anna May Wong in 1930, then reimagined by John Edmonds in Tête d’Homme in 2018. Richard Avedon, Cindy Sherman, Hiroshi Sugimoto, Dora Maar, Dorothea Lange… A true anthology, “Remember Me” showcases emblematic work and offers the public an ideal journey for the bicentenary.
“Remember Me” is on view at the Bourse de Commerce , in Paris, until January 18, 2027.
